questions.question_text: State the order of the differential equation $\left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=y^4$.

options.why: Read the power $3$ on the second derivative as the order; the power does not change the order.
Took the highest power of $y$ in the equation as the order instead of the highest derivative.
Used the lowest derivative present, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, rather than the highest.

questions.solution_text:
The derivatives present are $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
The power $3$ is on a derivative, not a new derivative, so it does not raise the order.
The highest derivative is $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so the order is $2$.

questions.question_text: Which of these equations is **not** a differential equation?

options.why: This does contain the derivative $y'$, so it is a differential equation of order $1$.
This does contain the derivative $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, so it is a differential equation of order $2$.
This does contain the derivative $y''$, so it is a differential equation of order $2$.

questions.solution_text:
A differential equation must contain a derivative.
$y^2+4y=x$ contains only powers of $y$ and $x$.
It is not a differential equation.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions is a solution of $xy'-2y=0$?

options.why: Added the constant to $x^2$ instead of multiplying; then $xy'-2y=-8$, not $0$.
Used $2$ as a multiplying coefficient of $x$ instead of the exponent; then $xy'-2y=-2x$.
Assumed every differential equation has an exponential solution, but here $xy'-2y=8xe^{2x}-8e^{2x}$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=4x^2$
$y'=8x$
LHS $=xy'-2y$
$=x(8x)-2\left(4x^2\right)$
$=8x^2-8x^2$
$=0$
RHS $=0$, so $y=4x^2$ is a solution.

questions.question_text: Which family of functions is the general solution of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y}{x}$ for $x\ne0$?

options.why: Here $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2Cx$ but $\dfrac{y}{x}=Cx$, so the two sides differ by a factor of $2$.
Here $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=Ce^{x}$ but $\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{Ce^{x}}{x}$, so the sides are not equal.
Here $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1$ but $\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{x+C}{x}$, which is $1$ only when $C=0$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=Cx$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=C$
RHS $=\dfrac{y}{x}$
$=\dfrac{Cx}{x}$
$=C$
LHS $=$ RHS for every constant $C$, so $y=Cx$ is the general solution.

questions.question_text:
Three of these functions satisfy $y''+9y=0$.
Which one does **not**?

options.why: This does satisfy the equation: $y''=-9\cos 3x$, so $y''+9y=0$.
This does satisfy the equation: $y''=-9\sin 3x$, so $y''+9y=0$.
This does satisfy the equation: $y''=-9y$ for this combination too, so $y''+9y=0$.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions is a solution of $y''-y'-12y=0$?

options.why: Changed the sign of the exponent without checking the equation; then $y''-y'-12y=8e^{-4x}$, not $0$.
Used the exponent $3$ without checking the first-derivative term; then $y''-y'-12y=-6e^{3x}$, not $0$.
Used the coefficient $12$ of $y$ as the exponent; then $y''-y'-12y=120e^{12x}$, not $0$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=e^{4x}$
$y'=4e^{4x}$
$y''=16e^{4x}$
LHS $=y''-y'-12y$
$=16e^{4x}-4e^{4x}-12e^{4x}$
$=0$
RHS $=0$, so $y=e^{4x}$ is a solution for every real $x$.

questions.question_text:
Verify whether $y=e^{5x}+e^{-x}$ is a solution of the initial value problem $y''-4y'-5y=0$ with $y(0)=2$ and $y'(0)=4$.
Which statement is correct?

options.text: It satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.
It satisfies the differential equation and $y(0)=2$, but $y'(0)=6$.
options.why: Differentiated $e^{-x}$ as $+e^{-x}$ instead of $-e^{-x}$; the correct value is $y'(0)=5-1=4$.

options.text: It satisfies both initial conditions, but $y''-4y'-5y=-2e^{-x}$.
options.why: Differentiated $-e^{-x}$ as $-e^{-x}$ instead of $+e^{-x}$, giving $y''=25e^{5x}-e^{-x}$ and the residual $-2e^{-x}$. The correct second derivative is $y''=25e^{5x}+e^{-x}$, which gives zero residual.

options.text: It satisfies the differential equation and $y'(0)=4$, but $y(0)=0$.
options.why: Treated the plus sign in $e^{5x}+e^{-x}$ as a minus sign when checking the initial value; actually $y(0)=1+1=2$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=e^{5x}+e^{-x}$
$y'=5e^{5x}-e^{-x}$
$y''=25e^{5x}+e^{-x}$
LHS $=y''-4y'-5y$
$=\left(25e^{5x}+e^{-x}\right)-4\left(5e^{5x}-e^{-x}\right)-5\left(e^{5x}+e^{-x}\right)$
$=(25-20-5)e^{5x}+(1+4-5)e^{-x}$
$=0$
RHS $=0$, so the differential equation is satisfied.
Check initial conditions:
$y(0)=1+1=2$
$y'(0)=5-1=4$
Therefore $y=e^{5x}+e^{-x}$ is a solution of the IVP.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions is a solution of $y''+4y=0$?

options.why: Used the $4$ from the equation as the coefficient of $x$; then $y''+4y=-36\cos 4x$.
Halved the $x$ instead of doubling it; then $y''+4y=\dfrac{45}{4}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}$.
Chose an exponential, but $y''=12e^{2x}$ is positive, so $y''+4y=24e^{2x}$.

questions.solution_text:
$y=3\cos 2x$
$y'=-6\sin 2x$
$y''=-12\cos 2x$
LHS $=y''+4y$
$=-12\cos 2x+4(3\cos 2x)$
$=-12\cos 2x+12\cos 2x$
$=0$
RHS $=0$, so $y=3\cos 2x$ is a solution.
